entries.citation: Bastani, H., Bastani, O., Sungu, A., Ge, H., Kabakcı, Ö., & Mariman, R. (2025). Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics. PNAS, 122(26), e2422633122. Correction (affiliation only): PNAS 122(34), e2518204122.

access.url: Europe PMC REST fullTextXML PMC12232635 (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); SI appendix via Europe PMC supplementaryFiles (pnas.2422633122.sapp.pdf); correction PMC12403119
sections_read: Version of record: Experimental Design; Main Results incl. Table 1; Student Perception; Heterogeneity; Robustness; Potential Mechanism incl. Table 2; Student Engagement; Discussion; footnotes (allocation, preregistration, consent)
SI A.4 Treatment Assignment and Covariate Balance incl. Table A.1
SI A.6 Pre-Registration Details incl. Tables A.2/A.3 (preregistered pairwise t-tests)
SI B.1 Non-compliance Table B.4/B.5; B.2 Table B.7 robustness; B.6 absenteeism
Correction notice PMC12403119: affiliation of one author only, no change to results
NOT read: AsPredicted registration text itself (4DL_Q3J), SI C.1-C.3 in detail, raw data/code on GitHub

entries.design: cluster-randomized field experiment, 3 arms (control / GPT Base / GPT Tutor), classroom = unit of allocation and of SE clustering; about fifty grade 9-11 classes; four 90-min sessions in Fall 2023; classes assigned to arms 'using an integer program' accounting for scheduling/laptop constraints plus student-count balance constraints (SI A.4); the main text describes the integer program as matching observable characteristics (footnote #); student-to-class assignment by the school is described as random except honors classes (excluded from main sample)
entries.population: high-school students grades 9-11, one large private-sector school in Ankara, Turkey; main sample 839 survey completers (Tutor 277, Control 320, Base 242; SI Table A.1); 943 incl. honors
entries.operation: symbolic_procedure (school mathematics review topics, e.g. combinatorics); exam items 'conceptually very similar' to practice items
entries.intervention: assisted practice phase with GPT-4 chat: GPT Base (standard tutor prompt with the problem) or GPT Tutor (prompt with teacher solutions, common mistakes and instruction to give hints, not answers); laptops supervised by teacher and staff
entries.comparator: business-as-usual practice with textbook and notes; solutions shown only after submission

outcome.measure: teacher-rubric normalized grade 0-1, graded by independent graders blinded to arm (SI A.5); practice (assisted) and exam (closed-book, unassisted)
outcome.assisted: practice phase assisted; primary preregistered outcome = unassisted exam
outcome.delay: none beyond the same 90-min session: exam immediately follows practice; no delayed retention test
outcome.transfer: near: each exam item paired with a conceptually very similar practice item

estimate.metric: ITT regression coefficient on normalized grade 0-1 (Table 1, class-clustered SE); relative % of control mean; preregistered pairwise difference with 95% CI (SI Table A.2)
estimate.value: Exam: GPT Base -0.054 (SE 0.022), GPT Tutor -0.004 (SE 0.013); control mean 0.321, SD 0.277. Practice: Base +0.137 (0.031), Tutor +0.361 (0.032); control mean 0.284. Relative: practice +48% / +127%, exam Base -17% (relative to control mean, NOT percentage points). Preregistered pairwise exam differences: Base vs Control -0.035 [-0.057, -0.012]; Tutor vs Control -0.006 [-0.030, 0.018]; Tutor vs Base +0.028 [0.005, 0.052]
estimate.ci: pairwise CIs as reported in SI Table A.2; Table 1 reports SE only
estimate.k_or_n: 2,848 student-session observations (Table 1); 839 students main sample; about fifty classes
estimate.note: R5 own arithmetic, not reported by authors: Tutor 95% interval from Table 1 approx. -0.004 +/- 1.96*0.013 = [-0.030, 0.021] on the 0-1 scale, i.e. about [-0.11, +0.08] control-SD units (normal approximation, ignores few-cluster small-sample correction). The Base exam effect -0.054 equals about -0.19 control SD. Non-significance of Tutor is NOT equivalence; whether it is non-inferior depends on a margin the study did not prespecify.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Strengths: preregistered primary outcome (unassisted exam), blinded independent grading, ITT, no differential absenteeism (12.3% average), robustness to honors inclusion/controls/clustering (SI B.2). Concerns: allocation is constrained (integer program) rather than a simple concealed random draw, and main text vs SI describe it differently (matching observables vs randomizing under constraints); few clusters (~50 over 3 arms) for class-level allocation; preregistered pairwise t-tests do not appear to cluster SEs; five class-sessions non-compliant; outcome is immediate and near (no delay, no novel transfer); GPT Tutor students could have answers checked during practice; GPT-4 of Fall 2023; single school, school mathematics, Turkey. Mechanism ('crutch') rests on non-preregistered exploratory error-rate and message-cluster analyses. Students' self-perceived learning did not track measured exam performance (SI B.3). Data and code public (GitHub obastani/GenAICanHarmLearning) -> reanalysis possible.

claim_edges.locator: Main Results Table 1; SI A.4, A.6 Table A.2: numbers confirmed; 'verhinderte den Schaden' is too strong: Tutor vs Control CI [-0.030, 0.018] does not establish non-inferiority without a margin; exam was immediate and near
Student Engagement Fig. 3; SI C.2 (help-seeking style differs by tool design)

entries.citation: Kestin, G., Miller, K., Klales, A., Milbourne, T., & Ponti, G. (2025). AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: An RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting. Scientific Reports, 15, 17458. Preprint v1: Research Square rs-4243877/v1, 14 May 2024, titled 'AI Tutoring Outperforms Active Learning'.

sections_read: VoR: Abstract; Results (post-test, time on task, regression, perceptions); Discussion; 'Context, limitations, and future directions'; Methods (population, course setting, study design, additional controls); footnotes; data availability

Supplement: Table S1 standardized regression coefficients; Table S2A group demographics; Table S4 description (item psychometrics); AI tutor system description incl. persona prompt and a question-specific prompt
Preprint v1: full text searched for N, coefficients, quantile range, discussion wording, limitations section
NOT read: GitHub study data; Table S2B/S3 content in detail (images)

entries.design: two-period crossover RCT in one course; students randomized to two groups (96 / 98) with peer-instruction groups (2-3 students) kept together, i.e. allocation at small-group level; each student had one AI-tutor lesson at home and one in-class active-learning lesson (topics surface tension, fluids); pre-test and post-test per lesson
entries.population: Harvard introductory physics for life sciences (PS2), Fall 2023; 233 enrolled, 194 eligible (consent, participation in both conditions, completion of all tests)
entries.operation: symbolic_procedure and conceptual physics (first exposure; items 33% analyzing, 41% applying, 21% understanding, 4% remembering per footnote)
entries.intervention: structured GPT-4-0613 tutor ('PS2 Pal') with expert persona prompt and question-specific step-by-step solutions, sequential scaffolding through problem parts, pre-recorded videos, self-paced at home; persona allows confirming answers and giving the answer if the student demands it
entries.comparator: in-class active learning lesson (peer instruction with staff support and instructor feedback) by the course instructors

outcome.measure: post-lesson quiz (not graded; participation credit), written by a separate team member from learning goals; item psychometrics reported in Table S4
outcome.assisted: post-test presumably without tutor; supervision of the AI-condition post-test at home is not described in the sections read
outcome.delay: immediate post-test after each lesson; no delayed test
outcome.transfer: same-lesson learning goals; no separate transfer measure

estimate.metric: standardized regression coefficient for condition (Table S1, student-clustered), plus quantile-regression range in SD units; medians
estimate.value: 0.63 (p < 0.001; R2 0.21); authors' quantile regression 0.73-1.3 SD; median post-score 4.5 (AI, N=142) vs 3.5 (in class, N=174), pre-test median 2.75 (N=316); median AI time on task 49 min vs 60 min assumed in class
estimate.ci: no CI reported for 0.63 in VoR or supplement
estimate.k_or_n: 194 eligible students; medians reported with N=142/174/316 post/pre scores
estimate.note: Internal inconsistency not explained in text read: 194 students x 2 lessons would give 388 post-tests, but medians use N=142 + 174 = 316. Same numbers appear in preprint v1. 0.63 is a covariate-adjusted standardized coefficient, not a raw Cohen d.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Version comparison: core numbers (194/233, 0.63, 0.73-1.3 SD, N 142/174/316, 49 min) identical in v1 and VoR. The VoR adds a 'Context, limitations, and future directions' section (first exposure, Bloom levels, dependence on expert prompts/videos/GPT-4; explicitly no presumption for complex synthesis/higher-order thinking), a note that authors overlap with those who established the in-class approach, FCI/CLASS subgroup statements and a supplement with item psychometrics; v1 headline 'learn more than twice as much' became 'learn significantly more in less time'. Risks: package comparison (medium, location, self-pacing, video, feedback all differ); unsupervised home condition vs class; low-stakes post-test; ceiling effect; no delayed or transfer outcome; exclusion of 39 non-eligible students conditional on completing both conditions; author-developer and instructor roles overlap; no CI for main estimate. Data public (GitHub HarvardAItutor/Study-Data-v4).

claim_edges.locator: VoR Results 'Learning gains: linear regression model'; Supplement Table S1; VoR 'Context, limitations, and future directions' (limitation wording verified in VoR, absent in v1)

entries.citation: Boolzen, C., Kuhn, J., Flegr, S., Rott, E., Stausberg, N., & Küchemann, S. (2026). Evidence of impact and interpretational limits of generative AI in STEM education: A systematic review and meta-analysis on cognitive learning outcomes. Artificial Intelligence Review, 59(10), 223.

entries.design: preregistered (AsPredicted 176450) systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis plus Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis (RoBMA), moderator and coincidence analysis; search ERIC, PsycINFO, Web of Science updated 7 May 2026; two pairs of independent raters
entries.population: mostly higher-education STEM learners; peer-reviewed quantitative studies after 2017 with comparison group
entries.operation: STEM knowledge and skills (externally assessed cognitive outcomes)
entries.intervention: learner interaction with generative AI, mostly text-based tools such as ChatGPT
entries.comparator: control/comparison groups as in primary studies; coded by ISAR level (inversion/substitution/augmentation/redefinition) relative to ICAP activity of control

outcome.assisted: unknown from abstract (whether tests were taken with AI not stated)
outcome.transfer: outcome type knowledge vs skills coded

estimate.metric: Hedges g (random effects); RoBMA bias-adjusted mean mu and heterogeneity tau
estimate.value: 85 eligible studies, 49 studies / 59 effect sizes meta-analysed; I2 = 96.32%; prediction interval g = -1.52 to 3.20; RoBMA mu = 0.076 +/- 0.254, tau = 1.190 +/- 0.166; moderators outcome type (R2 12.5%) and ISAR level (R2 13.0%) robust under bias correction
estimate.ci: unadjusted pooled g and its CI are not given in the abstract
estimate.note: Abstract states that the overall positive effect 'can be largely attributed to publication bias'; 33 studies reported large effects only because intervention and control cognitive activity were not comparable; substitution of learner activity described as potentially detrimental. Numbers as in abstract; the meaning of '+/-' (posterior SD) not verified in full text.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Strong design features (preregistration, dual coding, bias-adjusted model) but full text not read: unadjusted estimate, risk-of-bias tool, delay/assistance coding and the ISAR subgroup estimates unverified. Directly relevant population (higher education) and operation (STEM). Key decision relevance: a positive average effect of GenAI in STEM is not robust; activity comparability between arms explains part of large effects.

claim_edges.locator: abstract (RoBMA mu; ISAR moderator; non-comparable control activity in 33 studies)

entries.citation: Liu, J., Sweet, T., Chen, M. H., Engelberg, J., Masters, M. C., Clark, M., Persaud, A., Lancaster, A., Hollingsworth, J. K., & Rice, J. K. (2026). The effects of course-integrated AI tutoring on student performance and engagement: A randomized university trial. IZA Discussion Paper No. 18989, October 2026.
entries.design: group-randomized trial, Fall 2025; randomization of instructors within 13 blocks of same/similar courses (9 exact-match blocks); ITT with block fixed effects and student covariates, SE clustered by course-section; analysis plan registered on OSF after data collection but before analysis
entries.population: 2,379 undergraduates, 30 instructors, 34 course-sections, large U.S. public university, 11 of 12 schools/colleges; exact-match sample 22 instructors / 1,353 students; 3 non-activating treatment instructors removed from sample
entries.operation: mixed course learning across disciplines (STEM, humanities, social sciences)
entries.intervention: access to a course-integrated GPT-4o chatbot with retrieval over course materials (citations), instructor-configurable tutor vs direct-instruction mode (most used the default direct mode); no prescribed instructional integration
entries.comparator: same/similar course sections without the assistant (other AI tools available to all students)

outcome.measure: instructor-posted final grade (0-100) and letter grade (primary); homework score; LMS engagement
outcome.assisted: unknown: researchers did not know which assessments were proctored or AI-permitted
outcome.transfer: course grades, not a designed transfer test

estimate.metric: ITT coefficient in raw points and control-group SD units
estimate.value: exact-match sample with controls: final grade -4.12 points = -0.37 SD; letter grade -0.11 GPA points = -0.13 SD; homework n.s. Full sample: no significant adverse academic effect (text 5.2). LMS total participation about -0.9 SD in both samples. First-generation students: additional -2.87 points (-0.28 SD) in full sample
estimate.note: Only about 15% of treated students ever used the tool (13% exact match); 73.8% of 3,460 requests were direct-answer requests, feedback on own attempt 0.7%. Users and non-users in treated sections had similarly lower grades; IV estimates (-1.99 / -2.83 SD) judged implausible as tool effects by the authors.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Working paper. Few clusters (34 sections, fewer in exact match); adverse academic effect only in the exact-match subsample; analysis plan registered post data collection; student sorting imbalance across instructors; grades are instructor-specific and assessment conditions (proctored/AI use) unknown; survey response 18% with differential response. Internal inconsistencies in the text read: Discussion says a significant difference in the 'full-match' sample whereas 5.2 reports no significant full-sample effect; Discussion cites 7.6% feedback requests whereas 7.3 reports 0.7% (7.6% = navigation). Mechanism (permissive AI climate vs tool use) not identified. Highly relevant as university, multi-discipline, semester-long, naturalistic access condition.

claim_edges.locator: 5.2 Impact of VSA Access; 7.1 (access effect not explained by use)
Abstract; 5.2: university AI tutor access without instructional integration did not improve and in exact-match sections lowered grades

entries.citation: Wang, R. E., Ribeiro, A. T., Robinson, C. D., Loeb, S., & Demszky, D. (2024, rev. 2026). Tutor CoPilot: A human-AI approach for scaling real-time expertise. arXiv:2410.03017 (v3, 10 Oct 2026). Preregistration https://osf.io/8d6ha.

access.url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.03017v3 plus arXiv API metadata for v3 and v1 abstract
sections_read: Abstract v3 and v1 (via arXiv API)

entries.design: preregistered RCT randomizing tutors (not students) to access to an LLM tool that suggests expert-like moves to human tutors during live chat tutoring; spring 2024, about two months
entries.population: v3: 783 tutors with study sessions (388 treatment / 395 control; 900 initially randomized) and 1,013 grade 3-6 students below grade level in a large southern U.S. district (79% Hispanic, 67% economically disadvantaged). v1 abstract had reported 900 tutors and 1,800 students
entries.intervention: human tutor with on-demand AI suggestions (human-in-the-loop)
entries.comparator: human tutors without the tool (business as usual)

outcome.measure: session exit ticket pass (topic 'mastery') - proximal; end-of-year NWEA MAP (distal) in an exposure-based student-level analysis
outcome.assisted: exit ticket after tutoring within the session; MAP unassisted
outcome.delay: exit ticket immediate; MAP end of year
outcome.transfer: MAP is a standardized distal test

estimate.metric: percentage points of exit-ticket pass probability
estimate.value: +4 p.p. (p < .01); +9 p.p. for students of lower-rated tutors; end-of-year MAP: no statistically significant improvement (authors, Limitations; SI D)
estimate.note: Cost about $20 per tutor per year (authors). Students were not randomized; exposure varied by tutor matching.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Strong for proximal tutor behaviour and session outcome; distal achievement effect not shown. Exit ticket is a curriculum-progression gate, so it is a proximal and partly assisted-context measure. Version drift between v1 and v3 in sample counts illustrates why version of record must be tracked. Human-AI co-pilot design is not the same as a learner-facing autonomous tutor.

claim_edges.locator: Abstract v3; Limitations (no significant end-of-year MAP effect)

entries.citation: Henkel, O., Horne-Robinson, H., Kozhakhmetova, N., & Lee, A. (2024). Effective and scalable math support: Evidence on the impact of an AI-tutor on math achievement in Ghana. arXiv:2402.09809 (v2, 5 May 2024).
entries.design: school-level random assignment of 11 schools (5 treatment, 6 control); baseline Feb and endline Aug 2023; analysis by independent-samples t-test on individual growth scores (no adjustment for clustering reported in sections read)
entries.population: grades 3-8/9 students in Rising Academies schools, Ghana; 637 at baseline, 477 completed both tests (241 control, 236/237 treatment); abstract says approximately 1,000
entries.operation: symbolic_procedure (foundational numeracy and algebra, grades 3-5 Global Proficiency Framework)
entries.intervention: WhatsApp chat-based math tutor with NLP/LLM components, two 30-min sessions per week during study hall, additional to regular instruction
entries.comparator: regular study hall without the tutor (no matched extra practice)

outcome.measure: same 35-item assessment at baseline and endline for all grades
outcome.transfer: curriculum-level assessment; ceiling at baseline for older students

estimate.metric: Cohen d on growth scores (pooled SD over both conditions and time points, Morris)
estimate.value: 0.36 in text (abstract: 0.37); growth 5.13 vs 2.12 points
estimate.note: p < 0.001 from an individual-level t-test; with 11 clusters this p-value is not interpretable as design-based precision.

entries.bias_and_applicability: High risk: 11 clusters, unadjusted analysis, 25% attrition, same test twice, ceiling effects, extra practice time confounded with the AI component, year-1 preprint only. Shows feasibility of low-bandwidth chat tutoring in LMIC; does not show advantage of GenAI over equivalent non-AI practice.

entries.citation: De Simone, M., Tiberti, F., Barron Rodriguez, M., Manolio, F., Mosuro, W., & Dikoru, E. J. (2025). From chalkboards to chatbots: Evaluating the impact of generative AI on learning outcomes in Nigeria. World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11125.

entries.design: student-level lottery among volunteers (52% of eligible expressed interest) in nine senior secondary schools; ITT; differential attrition handled by Lee bounds and IPW; no preregistration found in text searched
entries.population: first-year senior secondary students, Benin City, Nigeria; 657 assigned treatment, 671 control; endline completed by 422 treatment and 337 control
entries.operation: recall_discrimination and language skills (English), plus AI knowledge and digital skills
entries.intervention: twelve 90-min after-school sessions over six weeks with Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4), teacher-guided prompts and peer work
entries.comparator: no program (business as usual; no extra session time)

outcome.measure: program-specific endline assessment (English, digital skills, AI skills, IRT composite) and regular third-term English exam
outcome.assisted: endline presumably without AI; not verified
outcome.delay: end of intervention; third-term exam later in term
outcome.transfer: third-term exam covered broader year content

estimate.value: overall 0.31 SD; English 0.23 (abstract) / 0.24 (intro) SD; AI skills 0.31; digital 0.14; IRT 0.26; third-term English exam 0.21 SD
estimate.note: Endline completion 64% treatment vs 50% control (own computation from counts); authors report significant differential attrition and positive Lee bounds.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Package effect (extra time, teachers, peers, AI) vs nothing; volunteers only; heavy differential attrition; partly program-aligned test; English abstract/intro figures differ slightly (0.23/0.24). Supports 'structured, teacher-guided extra practice with AI can help' but not AI-specific causality or comparison with direct LLM use.

entries.design: review of experiments comparing human tutoring, computer tutoring (answer-, step-, substep-based) and no tutoring
entries.population: mixed, mostly STEM experiments (details not verified)
entries.intervention: human tutoring; step-based ITS; answer-based CAI

estimate.value: human tutoring d = 0.79; ITS d = 0.76 (abstract); widely believed values 0.3/1.0/2.0 not confirmed
estimate.note: Step-based vs answer-based split values not verified in this run.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Abstract-level only. Comparison against 'no tutoring' with same content; mostly researcher-developed systems and aligned tests (see kulik2016, cheungslavin2016methods). Does not address generative AI or delayed unassisted transfer.

entries.citation: Kulik, J. A., & Fletcher, J. D. (2016). Effectiveness of intelligent tutoring systems: A meta-analytic review. Review of Educational Research, 86(1), 42-78.
entries.design: meta-analysis of 50 controlled evaluations; separate description of 6 evaluations with nonconventional controls and 4 with flawed implementations
entries.intervention: intelligent tutoring systems

outcome.measure: test scores; locally developed vs standardized

estimate.value: 0.66 SD median over 50 evaluations; much smaller on standardized than locally developed tests (values not in abstract); small effects with nonconventional controls or flawed implementations
estimate.note: Test alignment is the authors' stated critical determinant.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Abstract-level. Median of aligned and standardized tests mixes outcome types; supports treating locally developed in-product tests as inflated proxies.

entries.citation: Ma, W., Adesope, O. O., Nesbit, J. C., & Liu, Q. (2014). Intelligent tutoring systems and learning outcomes: A meta-analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology, 106(4), 901-918.
entries.design: meta-analysis, 107 effect sizes, 14,321 participants
entries.operation: procedural and declarative knowledge across domains
entries.intervention: ITS (as principal instruction, supplement, integral component or homework aid)
entries.comparator: teacher-led large group; non-ITS CBI; textbooks/workbooks; individual human tutoring; small-group instruction

estimate.value: vs teacher-led large group 0.42; vs non-ITS CBI 0.57; vs textbooks/workbooks 0.35; vs individual human tutoring -0.11 (n.s.); vs small-group instruction 0.05 (n.s.)
estimate.note: Authors judge findings consistent with their publication-bias analysis.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Abstract-level; outcome alignment and delay not verifiable; pre-LLM ITS.

entries.citation: Steenbergen-Hu, S., & Cooper, H. (2013). A meta-analysis of the effectiveness of intelligent tutoring systems on K-12 students' mathematical learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 105(4), 970-987.
entries.design: meta-analysis of 26 reports / 34 independent samples (1997-2010)
entries.intervention: ITS, mostly vs regular classroom instruction
entries.comparator: regular classroom; few vs homework or human tutoring

estimate.value: average g = 0.01 to 0.09; larger for interventions shorter than a school year; larger for general population than low achievers
estimate.note: Explicit null-to-small result for K-12 math field use.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Abstract-level. Disconfirming observation for optimistic ITS averages: longer real-world deployments in K-12 math show near-zero average effects; potential widening of achievement gap.

entries.citation: Aleven, V., Roll, I., McLaren, B. M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2016). Help helps, but only so much: Research on help seeking with intelligent tutoring systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26(1), 205-223.

entries.intervention: real-time feedback on help-seeking behaviour (Help Tutor)

outcome.delay: help-seeking change persisted after feedback stopped

estimate.value: more deliberate help use, persisting after feedback ended; no better domain learning outcomes
estimate.note: Authors no longer view on-demand help as important as they once did but still recommend it in some circumstances.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Abstract-level. Null for domain learning from metacognitive help-seeking feedback; relevant to whether a tutor should coach help seeking.

entries.citation: Pane, J. F., Griffin, B. A., McCaffrey, D. F., & Karam, R. (2014). Effectiveness of Cognitive Tutor Algebra I at scale. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 36(2), 127-144.

entries.population: middle and high school Algebra I students
entries.intervention: Cognitive Tutor Algebra I (personalized, mastery-learning, blended curriculum) under naturalistic adoption conditions

estimate.value: year 1: no effects; year 2: positive, significant for high schools, not for middle schools; about eight percentile points for the median student

entries.bias_and_applicability: Abstract-level; large-scale, independent outcome; implementation learning curve.

entries.citation: Roschelle, J., Feng, M., Murphy, R. F., & Mason, C. A. (2016). Online mathematics homework increases student achievement. AERA Open, 2(4).

sections_read: impact results incl. effect size paragraph and Table 2/3 notes

entries.design: school-level random assignment within matched pairs (40 paired + 3 unpaired schools), two-level HLM; impact measured in the second school year after a year of teacher implementation
entries.intervention: ASSISTments online homework with immediate feedback and hints plus teacher reports and training

estimate.value: 0.18 (adjusted difference 8.84 scale points); larger for students with lower prior achievement
estimate.note: School-level attrition 6.5%, differential 3.8% (within WWC standards per authors).

entries.bias_and_applicability: Strong independent standardized outcome and cluster design; rural homogeneous state with universal laptops; effect includes teacher-facing reports and training, so not a pure student-hint effect.

entries.citation: Pelánek, R. (2017). Bayesian knowledge tracing, logistic models, and beyond: An overview of learner modeling techniques. User Modeling and User-Adapted Interaction, 27(3-5), 313-350.

sections_read: 6.1 Metrics for Model Comparison incl. Table 3

entries.design: narrative overview of learner modeling (BKT, logistic models, extensions), framed by KLI
entries.intervention: learner models feeding instructional policies (mastery learning, item sequencing, spacing)
entries.comparator: simple heuristics such as 'k correct in a row'

outcome.measure: predictive accuracy metrics (RMSE, LL, AUC) vs policy impact

estimate.value: unknown
estimate.note: Key statements: advantage of learner modeling for mastery policies 'not yet completely clear' (3.2); AUC not meaningful if policy uses absolute probabilities (6.1); small accuracy gains often negligible but can change decisions; prefer simple learner models unless clear reason (7.1).

entries.bias_and_applicability: Accepted manuscript, not version of record (page numbers may differ). Expert narrative; directly relevant to whether Mastery needs probabilities.

entries.citation: Pelánek, R. (2018). Conceptual issues in mastery criteria: Differentiating uncertainty and degrees of knowledge. In Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED 2018), Lecture Notes in Computer Science, pp. 450-461. Springer.
entries.design: model proposal (LogisticHMM) plus simulation comparison of mastery criteria
entries.intervention: mastery criterion separating degree of knowledge and uncertainty
entries.comparator: N consecutive correct; exponential moving average; BKT with 0.95 threshold

outcome.measure: agreement of mastery decisions with simulated ground truth

estimate.value: with low observation noise, NCC with suitable N gives nearly the same decisions; NCC worse under noisy observations; author does not expect the new model to change real decisions significantly
estimate.note: Reading BKT >= 0.95 as '95% certainty of mastery' is misleading unless data match BKT's strong assumptions.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Simulation only, single author; strong conceptual support for reporting degree (e.g. unassisted success share) and evidence amount (attempts) separately instead of one probability.

entries.citation: Gervet, T., Koedinger, K., Schneider, J., & Mitchell, T. (2020). When is deep learning the best approach to knowledge tracing? Journal of Educational Data Mining, 12(3), 31-54.
entries.design: empirical comparison of learner performance models on nine real-world datasets, cross-validation across students, ablations, calibration analysis
entries.intervention: logistic regression with features, DKT, BKT and other Markov models

outcome.transfer: no cross-validation in item space (authors' main limitation)

estimate.value: LR best on moderate data; DKT best on large or time-sensitive data; BKT lags; models calibrated only in data-dense intervals, e.g. assistments09 severe over/underestimation at extremes
estimate.note: Authors: weakest links are usually the instructional policy and KC model, not the predictor; models with similar accuracy can make vastly different recommendations.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Predictive benchmarking only; no learning outcome. Mastery has no data of this size; supports abstention from calibrated probabilities.

entries.citation: Khajah, M., Lindsey, R. V., & Mozer, M. C. (2016). How deep is knowledge tracing? Proceedings of the 9th International Conference on Educational Data Mining. arXiv:1604.02416.
entries.design: model comparison on tutoring datasets
entries.intervention: BKT extended with forgetting, skill discovery, individual abilities

estimate.value: extended BKT performance indistinguishable from DKT
estimate.note: Per pelanek2017 6.1, AUC averaging choices had inflated earlier DKT advantages.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Predictive accuracy only; supports 'depth not needed' for KT; venue details from arXiv metadata, not verified against proceedings.

entries.citation: Kraft, M. A. (2020). Interpreting effect sizes of education interventions. Educational Researcher, 49(4), 241-253. (EdWorkingPaper 19-10, 2019, read.)

access.url: https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED602384.pdf (working-paper version, ERIC ED602384); journal version not read; journal bibliographic data verified via Crossref
sections_read: Guideline 2 (what, when, how outcomes are measured)

entries.design: methodological guidance plus empirical distribution of 1,942 effect sizes from 747 RCTs with standardized achievement outcomes
entries.intervention: n/a

estimate.value: benchmarks: < 0.05 small, 0.05 to < 0.20 medium, >= 0.20 large; median 0.10 SD; researcher-designed aligned tests often 2-4 times larger effects than broad standardized tests
estimate.note: Benchmarks are for K-12 standardized outcomes, not for university or in-product tests.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Working-paper text read; journal bibliographic data verified via Crossref, journal text not read. Useful to justify small non-inferiority margins and to discount aligned/proximal in-product measures.

entries.citation: Cheung, A. C. K., & Slavin, R. E. (2016). How methodological features affect effect sizes in education. Educational Researcher, 45(5), 283-292.

entries.intervention: n/a (methodological moderators)

estimate.value: roughly twice as large for published, small-scale and experimenter-made measures vs unpublished, large-scale, independent measures; quasi-experiments larger than RCTs
estimate.note: Journal bibliographic data verified via Crossref.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Abstract-level; directly relevant to discounting in-product, small-sample, developer-made measures.
